question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$
